'''''Eucalyptus nitens''''', commonly known as '''shining gum''' or '''silvertop''',<ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus nitens'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_nitens.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=31 May 2020}}</ref> is a species of tall tree native to Victoria and eastern New South Wales. It has smooth greyish bark, sometimes with thin, rough bark near the base, lance-shaped adult leaves, flower buds in groups of seven or nine, white flowers and cup-shaped, barrel-shaped or cylindrical fruit. It grows in wet forests and rainforest margins on fertile soils in cool, high-rainfall areas.

==Description==
''Eucalyptus nitens'' is a tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|70|m}}, sometimes to {{cvt|90|m}} in Victoria, and does not form a [[lignotuber]]. It has smooth white, grey or yellow bark, often with persistent, rough, fibrous or flaky greyish bark near the base. The smooth bark is shed in long ribbons. Young plants have [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]] leaves arranged in opposite pairs, lance-shaped to egg-shaped or heart-shaped, {{cvt|65-110|mm}} long and {{cvt|28-55|mm}} wide with stem-clasping bases. Adult leaves are lance-shaped to curved, glossy green, sometimes slightly paler on the lower surface, {{cvt|100-300|mm}} long and {{cvt|15-40|mm}} wide, tapering to a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|10-40|mm}} long. The flower buds are arranged in leaf [[wikt:axil|axil]]s in groups of seven on an unbranched [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|5-15|mm}} long, the individual buds sessile. Mature buds are oval or cylindrical, {{cvt|6-7|mm}} long and {{cvt|3-4|mm}} wide with a conical [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]] that is the same width as the [[Hypanthium|floral cup]] but shorter than it. Flowering occurs from January to March and the flowers are white. The fruit is a woody cylindrical, cup-shaped or barrel-shaped [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|4-7|mm}} long and wide with the valves near rim level.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name=boland>Boland, D. J. ''et al.'': Forest Trees of Australia. CSIRO Publishing, Collingwood</ref><ref name=brooker>Brooker, M. I. H. & Kleinig, D. A. 2006: Field Guide to Eucalypts, Volume 1 South-eastern Australia. Bloomings Books, Melbourne</ref><ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=Ken |title=''Eucalyptus nitens'' |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Eucalyptus~nitens |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden, Sydney |access-date=13 November 2019}}</ref><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus nitens'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20nitens |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=13 November 2019}}</ref><ref name="RBGV">{{cite web |last1=Brooker |first1=M. ==Taxonomy and naming==
Shining gum was first formally described in 1899 by [[Henry Deane (engineer)|Henry Deane]] and [[Joseph Maiden]], who gave it the name ''Eucalyptus goniocalyx'' var. ''nitens'' and published the description in ''[[Linnean Society of New South Wales|Proceedings of the Linnean Society of New South Wales]]''.<ref name=APNI1>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus goniocalyx'' var. ''nitens''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/454680|publisher=APNI|access-date=13 November 2019}}</ref><ref name="Deane">{{cite journal |last1=Deane |first1=Henry |last2=Maiden |first2=Joseph |title=Observation on the eucalypts of New South Wales, Part V |journal=Proceedings of the Linnean Society of New South Wales |date=1899 |volume=24 |issue=3 |page=463 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/21735#page/561/mode/1up |access-date=13 November 2019}}</ref> In 1913, Maiden raised the variety to species status as ''E. nitens'', publishing the change in his book, ''A Critical Revision of the Genus Eucalyptus''.<ref name=APNI2>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus nitens''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/455051|publisher=APNI|access-date=13 November 2019}}</ref><ref name="Maiden">{{cite book |last1=Maiden |first1=Joseph |title=A Critical Revision of the Genus Eucalyptus |date=1913 |publisher=New South Wales Government Printer |location=Sydney |pages=272–274 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/100166#page/388/mode/1up |access-date=13 November 2019}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''nitens'') is a [[Latin]] word meaning "shining", referring to the leaves, flower buds, fruit and bark of this species.<ref name="CANBR" />

==Distribution==
''Eucalyptus nitens'' occurs in Victoria on ranges east and north-east of Melbourne at high altitudes on the east of the Great Dividing Range from the Blue Range, Mt Monda and Mt Torbreck eastwards. It is also found on the high tablelands and mountains of southern New South Wales. There are two widely disjunct populations at high altitude (around {{cvt|1500|m}}) at [[Barrington Tops]] and near [[Ebor, New South Wales|Ebor]] in north eastern New South Wales.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Field guide to eucalypts|last=Brooker, M. I. H. (M. Ian H.)|date=2006|publisher=Bloomings Books|others=Kleinig, D. A.|isbn=1876473525|edition= 3rd|page=188|location=Melbourne|oclc=76889530}}</ref>

==Uses==
In [[Tasmania]] ''Eucalyptus nitens'' is one of the most important [[plantation]] tree species along with ''[[Eucalyptus globulus]]'' (Tasmanian blue gum) and ''[[Pinus radiata]]'' (Monterey pine). As of 2021, Tasmania had around 210,000 hectares of nitens plantations, established for use in pulp mills. After the closure of the mills, they have typically been exported as woodchips, although in the 2020s there have been efforts to create engineered wood products.<ref>{{cite web | url= https://www.abc.net.au/news/rural/2021-09-11/new-purpose-for-eucalyptus-nitens/100439916 | title=Worth more than woodchips? Finding another future for Tasmania's eucalyptus nitens | date=11 September 2021 | last=Bennett | first=Lachlan | publisher=ABC News}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2023-08-08/tasmania-s-first-timber-high-rise-building-under-construction/102696848 | title=Tasmania's first timber high-rise building taking shape on Launceston skyline | date=9 August 2023 | last=Breen | first=Fiona | publisher=ABC News}}</ref> The timber can be used in general construction but is beginning to be used in furniture where the discolourations may be a feature.<ref>[http://www.vwa.org.au/des_vichard_sg.htm VWA page] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100113052504/http://www.vwa.org.au/des_vichard_sg.htm |date=2010-01-13 }} Victorian Woodworkers Association</ref>

==Possible toxicity==
Extracts from ''Eucalyptus nitens'' leaves have been found to be toxic to mollusc larvae.<ref name="Australian Story staff">{{Cite web |url=http://www.abc.net.au/austory/specials/somethingwatertwo/default.htm |title=Australian Story :: Something In The Water - Part 2 |publisher=Australian Broadcasting Corporation |author=Australian Story staff}}</ref> However, this study did not compare the toxicity of ''Eucalyptus nitens'' with other species and it is not known if it is any more or less toxic than other eucalypts.  [[Eucalyptus oil]], which is extracted from the leaves of eucalypts, is known to be toxic and have antiseptic properties.

Toxicological studies (in six laboratories) reported on the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's Australian Story program Feb 2010<ref name="Australian Story staff"/><ref name="ABCAustralianStory">{{Cite web |url=http://www.abc.net.au/austory/specials/somethingwater/default.htm |title=Australian Story :: Something In The Water - Part 1 |publisher=Australian Broadcasting Corporation |author=Australian Story staff}}</ref> found that the surface scum (foam) collected from a river supplying water to a Tasmanian town kills water fleas, mollusc larvae and human cell lines, and it was reported on the same program that "a large increase in cancer sufferers and a lot of people with rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma, lupus" might have the same cause.<ref name="ABCAustralianStory"/>  However, studies commissioned by the Tasmanian Department of Health and Human Services found no reliable evidence that people who source water from this river are less healthy than people living elsewhere.<ref name="St Helens Drinking Water">{{Cite web |url=http://www.dhhs.tas.gov.au/news_and_media/?a=50980 |title= St Helens Drinking Water |author=Tasmanian Department of Health and Human Services}}</ref> Furthermore, although the Australian Story programs implied that ''Eucalyptus nitens'' plantations were the source of the toxins (which initiated widespread claims that such plantations represented 'toxic plantations' or 'poisonous plantations'), foam samples from native forest catchments devoid of both plantations and ''Eucalyptus nitens'' had previously been found to be similarly toxic.<ref name="George River Water Quality Panel">{{Cite web |url=http://www.georgeriverwater.org.au/ |title=George River Water Quality Panel |author=George River Water Quality Panel |access-date=2010-07-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101003082423/http://www.georgeriverwater.org.au/ |archive-date=2010-10-03 |url-status=dead }}</ref>  These natural toxins are highly concentrated (approximately 1400 fold) in river foam.<ref name="George River Water Quality Panel"/>

The claims and all available scientific data relating to the issue were reviewed by an Environment Protection Authority appointed group (established by Premier Bartlett) of eminent scientists from the University of Tasmania, Griffith University, Monash University and CSIRO in the first half of 2010.<ref name="George River Water Quality Panel"/>  It was conclusively found by them that the water quality of the George River is of excellent standard, the cancer rates within the catchment are no higher than the Tasmanian average, and that any concern raised regarding the toxins in water foam was largely due to erroneous sampling techniques in the aforementioned toxicological studies. In June 2011 an internal ABC investigation found that the programs in question fell short of ABC editorial standards relating to contextual accuracy and balance.<ref name="ABC Managing Directors summary">{{Cite web |url=http://www.abc.net.au/austory/content/2011/s3248506.htm |title= ABC Managing Directors summary|author=Mark Scott}}</ref>

After the Australian Story went to air the Tasmanian Director of Public Health, Dr Roscoe Taylor, had had an activated carbon purification system added to the St Helens water treatment plant. Dr Taylor stated at the time of its installation that "No scientific evidence has been presented to confirm the drinking water in St Helens was unsafe for human health before this precaution was taken".<ref name="Update on St Helens drinking water">{{Cite web |url=http://www.dhhs.tas.gov.au/news_and_media/?a=52086 |title= Update on St Helens drinking water|author=Taylor, Legge and Cash}}</ref> The filter was not removed after the review panel published its report.<ref name="George River Water Quality Panel"/>

The rebuttal of the George River Water's Panels deliberations on the scientists research and findings (NIWA's scientist, Dr Chris Hickey) sent to the ABC in July 2010 was posted on the ABC website at the time of the ABC's managing director's statement in June 2011.
